text:
carla: Quick RFC follow-up — private control plane split + egress handling. I sketched a migration plan that favors a regional relay for early GA, then a gradual opt-in to per-tenant ephemeral egress when customers need IP preservation. Putting notes and open questions below.

samir: +1 on regional relay as default. simplest for onboarding. what are the concrete tradeoffs we should call out?

carla: tradeoffs I'm listing: operational complexity, cost (per-tenant IP pools vs shared NAT), failure modes (relay saturation vs per-tenant NAT exhaustion), observability surface (harder to attribute tokens to customer when NATing).

jeni: also watch TLS/auth bootstrapping. regional relay needs a lightweight agent in customer VPC to handshake. we must define retry/heartbeat semantics. current agent does 30s keepalive which caused weird reconnections in staging.

mike: for handshake we should use mutual TLS with cert provisioning from control plane. agent flow: agent -> controlplane (outbound mTLS) to fetch relay endpoints, agent registers local egress cidrs. That avoids inbound rules.

nate: question: how do we do source IP preservation for customers on the Dedicated plan who require static egress? per-tenant elastic IP allocation?

carla: yes, for Dedicated customers we offer static EIPs pinned to their relay(s). For hosted/private customers who want stable IPs but not full dedicated infra, we propose an "ephemeral-pool with pinning" model: customer requests pin, we map them a stable mapping in the relay for a TTL.

samir: TTL pinning seems risky if customers expect long-lived IPs. need migration story to move pins between relays during maintenance without breaking upstream allowlists.

carla: agreed. propose a dual-path: support a proxy-level header X-Forwarded-For and also maintain a controlplane-side mapping service that can swap pinned IPs atomically and emit rotation events so customers can be notified.

jeni: on the agent side, we should expose a small config toggle so customers can declare "preserve_source: required|optional". default required=false. sample config: 
```
agent.config: 
  controlplane.mode: regional-relay
  egress: 
    preserve_source: optional
    pin_ttl_seconds: 86400
    mtls: true
```

mike: + sample looks good. do we have metrics defined for when a relay is saturating? I want token_per_second, conn_rps, pinned_ip_count, nat_table_utilization.

carla: add those to the console dashboard plan. also add a per-customer egress-cost estimate: pinned IPs have a fixed monthly amortized cost.

nate: migration plan? how do we move existing customers on peering+private endpoints to the relay model without downtime?

carla: rough steps: 
1) Offer relay as opt-in beta, run in parallel with peering. agent supports both (agent can route selected subnets to relay).
2) Add observability hooks and traffic mirroring for validation.
3) Run canaries where small % traffic uses relay; monitor p99 latency, error rate.
4) Gradual traffic shift, inform customers to update allowlists for relay egress IPs.
5) For customers requiring stable IPs, allocate pinned IPs and test connectivity.
6) Cutover and deprecate old peering paths after customer signoff.

samir: sounds reasonable. what's the canary mechanism? feature flag in controlplane to steer X% of requests to relay for a given tenant?

carla: exactly. controlplane routing policy: route_policy: {type: canary, percent: 5, start_time: ...}. We'll surface that in the Console rollout page.

deploy-bot: canary deployment for cp-relay v2 started: rollout_id=crv2-2024-10-18-1, initial_region=us-west-2.

jeni: ops note: agent upgrade must be backwards compatible. if older agents don't understand preserve_source, they should default to previous behavior. Add server-side guarding so we don't attempt pinned IP assignment for unsupported agents.

mike: another opt: instead of per-tenant pinned IPs we could offer per-customer NAT gateways inside the relay VPC (one per customer). easier semantics at cost of more infra. pros/cons?

carla: pros: predictable, easier to reason about. cons: cost and scaling complexity for many small customers. we'll reserve per-customer NAT for enterprise tier.

nate: what about DNS and TLS? Some customers do IP-based allowlists and also verify TLS SANs. we must keep TLS cert chain stable during rotation and provide guidance for DNS TTLs.

carla: note: recommend customers allowlist both IPs and set TTLs >= 300s while we do rotation events. We'll add docs and a rollout checklist.

samir: outstanding engineering tasks? I'll list them: 
- relay autoscaling: add backpressure metrics and queue shedding policy
- mapping service: pin/unpin API + audit logs
- agent handshake retry backoff bump to 60s behind a feature flag
- console: per-tenant egress summary + cost estimate

carla: add compliance tasks: logging retention for pinned IP mapping, KMS keys for pin metadata, and SOC2 doc updates.

jeni: Ops runbook items: 
- how to detect NAT table exhaustion (metric: nat_table_utilization > 0.9)
- mitigation: spin up relay instance pool, notify customer, provision temporary EIP and update mapping
- rollback: steer traffic back to peering via controlplane route policy

mike: I'll prototype mapping service API this week. thoughts on data model? simple: {customer_id, pinned_ip, expires_at, assigned_relay, audit_user}.

carla: that works. ensure audit_user accepts system-generated events for rotation. Also store history for at least 90 days.

sre-bot: alert rule suggestion: ALERT RelayNatHighUtilization IF nat_table_utilization > 0.9 FOR 5m LABELS {severity="pg-1"} ANNOTATIONS {summary="Relay NAT near capacity"}

carla: final note: we'll file a follow-up RFC that includes the migration checklist, API shapes, and rollout timeline. target: 6-week rollout for beta. I'll create the RFC and ping infra + devex.

samir: thanks — I can help draft the autoscaling and canary sections.

jeni: I'll do the agent change and runbook.

mike: mapping service PR will reference this thread.

carla: perfect — I'll update the RFC draft and link back here. :raised_hands:
